content.text:
**No.** With this project and these tools, I can't give you real 3D swimming that stays faithful to your approved pictures from start to end with no visible differences. Here are the straight answers.

**1. Can I achieve both?** No. Your approved screen is one painting seen from one spot. Real 3D swimming needs a whole tunnel that can be seen from every position along the way. Everything your painting doesn't show (the sides, what's ahead, what's behind) has to be built or generated, and that part never matches the painting exactly. Every attempt in this project shows the same thing. The still painted screen measured about 94% like your picture. Every version where the camera really moves through 3D measured about 5–12%.

**2. Is there a technical solution different from what failed?** There is one thing not yet tried properly, and I can't promise it works. It uses World Labs Atlas, which is already connected. Atlas would generate many views travelling down your tunnel from your picture, then combine them into a photographic-style 3D scene. Benny would swim through it with a real follow-camera, with real flowing water and coins added on top. In November the project tried a simpler version, a 3D world made from your single picture. The far third of the tunnel and the S-curved river collapsed, so it wasn't usable. The multi-view method is the step up from that. Otherwise the industry answer is a dedicated 3D environment artist who builds the tunnel by hand in Blender from your painting.

**3. What differences would remain, even if it works?**
- Details further down the tunnel would be invented, not yours.
- Close-up areas could look soft or blurry.
- The glow and lighting would be flatter than the painting.
- The water would be animated, not your exact painted streaks.
- The S-curves may not follow your painting exactly.
- It might have to be simplified to run smoothly on cheaper Android phones.

**4. Can I demonstrate it on one short section of Screen 05 first?** Yes, but it costs World Labs credits. Before spending anything I would give you the exact job and credit cost and wait for your OK. I won't touch other screens unless it works on that section.

**5. What can't I deliver?** "Exactly my approved screen in every frame of genuine 3D gameplay" is beyond what I can build. A 3D environment artist would come closer than I can, but even then it would match your art in style, not pixel for pixel. Anything better than "clearly your screen, with visible differences" would be a guess, not a promise.

Everything you have is saved and unchanged:
- the painted version, `?paint=1`
- both Benny-swimming tests
- the rejected 3D version

Do you want me to quote the credit cost for the one-section Screen 05 test? If not, I'll stop here.

Base directory for this skill: /root/.claude/plugins/cache/worldlabs/worldlabs/0.2.2/skills/atlas-splats

# Atlas splats

`posedImages2Splats` reconstructs a scene from posed views with depth, then refines it into an
SPZ file. It is the final step, and one run takes 15 to 25 minutes.
While refining it generates its own dense views, which it does not return.

What you control is the set of views you give it, so a good result comes from getting that set
right. The views are also the preview of the result.

This file and [references/scene.md](references/scene.md) are the method, and the request shapes
are in `assets/example/`. Read both files in full before starting. The Atlas docs are reference
for a task's fields and limits: open a task's page when a request needs a field these files do
not show, or when one is rejected. The docs also have shorter workflow pages written for people;
where they differ from these files, follow these files.

## Steps

1. **Agree where to work, then build the scene.** Before anything else, check whether Blender
   is installed and ask the person where to work. With Blender installed, the choice is:

   - **Open Blender**, so they can watch the scene build and scrub through it; or
   - **Build in the background** and hand over the `.blend` at the end.

   If they choose the open window, open it as soon as the first image is posed, before any
   views or path, so they watch from the start. Without Blender, work in the shell.
   [references/scene.md](references/scene.md) has the question for each setup and the steps:
   pose the images, build the scene out in rounds of a few views until it is blocked out with no
   gaps, and show it.

2. **Check the set as reconstruction input.** The posed frames and the views you kept are the
   input. A good set:

   - shows every area the person will look at: the floor, low furniture, walls, and the far side
     of anything they will move around. Areas no view shows come out blurry or invented;
   - agrees with itself. An object with a different shape or place in two views becomes a
     doubled, ghosted object;
   - has depth over most of every frame, and one size for all frames. A view can look right and
     still have depth on only a small part of it.

   For a single room, 12 to 16 views in all is a good range. To add coverage, send another
   `atlasGenerate` request with the current views as `contextFrames` and `"returnDepth": true`.

3. **Reconstruct once.** Submit it as soon as the set is good, and tell the person it is
   running and how long it takes. The request lists each frame's image, depth and camera; see
   [the example request](assets/example/splats-request.json).

   ```sh
   worldlabs tasks run posedImages2Splats --request splats.json --json > splats_op.json
   worldlabs operations wait <operation-id> --timeout 3600 --json
   ```

   Submit without `--wait` and keep the operation ID. If the wait times out, wait again. A
   second submission while the first runs starts a second full run.

4. **Hand it over.**

   ```sh
   worldlabs operations download <operation-id> --out splats
   ```

   The result is an SPZ file named for its splat count (`refinedSplats_2000000.spz`), in the
   same world as the cameras you sent. Look at it before you report: from the start view, and
   from places the person will go.

   Give the person the file, a way to look at it, the operation ID, and which parts of the scene
   the model invented. In Blender the splats import into the scene they have been watching.
   Otherwise see [Rendering with Spark](https://docs.atlas.worldlabs.ai/rendering-with-spark.md).

## Example

[A complete run](references/example.md): one photo of a potter's studio, the room built out in
three rounds of views, and one reconstruction from the ten frames, with pictures of the result.
Its requests and results are in `assets/example/`. It shows one scene's choices, not values to
copy.

## Facts

- Bounded, textured interiors reconstruct best. Sky, foliage, thin structures, glass, faces and
  large plain walls are where artifacts appear, and so are surfaces that only one view sees at
  close range. Say so when the scene has them.
- `prompt` describes the scene. Leave it out and Atlas writes one from the images.
- For a mesh, pass the SPZ asset to `splats2Mesh` as `splatAsset`.
- A video of the same scene uses the same views; see the `atlas-flythrough` skill.
- An HTTP 422 means the request was rejected. The CLI does not print the reason; check that
  every frame has `imageAsset`, `depth.depthAsset` and `camera`, and that all cameras share one
  size.
- CLI setup, errors and other tasks are in the `worldlabs-cli` skill. Guides:
  https://docs.atlas.worldlabs.ai/posed-images-to-splats.md and
  https://docs.atlas.worldlabs.ai/splat-best-practices.md

content.content:
with the same request and `--idempotency-key <key>` so the task is not started twice.
- **Result.** A finished operation has `response` or `error`; check `error` first.
  `operations download` saves every output file to a new directory, named for its place in the
  response (`frames_003_image.jpg`, `frames_003_depth.exr`), and writes `operation.json` with
  each file's local path. If the command is missing, update the CLI.
- **Errors.** The CLI does not print the API's reason. HTTP 422 means the request body was
  rejected: check it against the task's guide page. HTTP 402 means the project is out of credits
  or over its spend limit. HTTP 401 or 403 is the key or its permissions. An operation that ends
  `THROTTLED` hit a capacity limit, not a problem with the request: tell the person, wait a few
  minutes, and run it again. See https://docs.atlas.worldlabs.ai/errors.md

Tasks spend the project's credits. Run the tasks the request needs without quoting prices or
asking for a go-ahead; https://docs.atlas.worldlabs.ai/billing.md has the rates if the person
asks. Do not rerun a finished task to see whether the result changes.

## Without a shell

If World Labs tools are connected (`list_projects` and a tool per task, such as
`images2PosedRGBD`), they run the same tasks. A task's tool takes `project_id`,
`idempotency_key`, and `request`, the same request body the task's guide page gives.

----
# Build the scene

A video and splats start the same way: agree how to work, pose the images, and build the scene
out a few views at a time until it is blocked out with no gaps. This file is identical in
`atlas-flythrough` and `atlas-splats`.

Building the scene is also a job on its own. When the person asks for new angles of an image,
the other side of something, or more of a place, do it this way, starting with where to work,
whether or not they have chosen a video or splats yet. Views that already exist from earlier in
the session are the start of the scene: bring them in and keep building from there.

Camera and depth conventions are in [conventions.md](conventions.md). A complete run is in
[example.md](example.md).

## Agree how to work

The person directs and you do the work. Two decisions are theirs:

- **Where the work happens.** Blender is the preferred place when it is installed. Both of you
  see the scene in 3D, they can shape the result, and they keep a project file at the end.
- **What the result should be.** The subject, how far the camera goes, what they want to be able
  to look at.

Asking is the default for those two. Ask each in one short line when it comes up. A plain
request, such as "make me a flythrough", is not a request to skip the questions.

Once they are settled, carry the work through to the finished result without stopping. Show
each stage as it lands (the posed image, each round of views, the path) so the person can steer
whenever they want to. They have asked for the result, so the steps that produce it need no
go-ahead and no price quoted.

Decide for the person only when they say outright that they do not want to be asked, for example
"don't check in, just deliver it". Then choose what they would most likely choose, and say what
you chose. For where to work, that is Blender in the background whenever it is installed.

Where to work comes first, before posing or reading further. Check what is there, then ask the
question that fits:

| What you find | What to ask |
| --- | --- |
| Blender 5.3 or newer, connected (it is open and you can run Python in it through Blender tools), with the Atlas add-on | Work in the open window where they can watch, or in the background and hand over the project at the end? |
| Blender installed, but the Blender tools or the Atlas add-on missing | Set that up now, or work in the background with what is there? Background work needs neither. |
| No Blender | Nothing. Work in the shell, and mention once that Blender would let both of you see the scene in 3D. |

Put the question in the person's terms: what each choice lets them see, and what it needs from
them. Words like "connected" describe your side of it and mean little to them. For example:
"Blender is installed. I can build this in an open Blender window so you can watch it take
shape, which needs Blender open and takes me a minute to link up, or build it in the background
and give you the Blender file at the end. Which would you like?"

`blender --version`, or `/Applications/Blender.app` on a Mac, tells you whether it is installed.
The `atlas-blender` skill covers working in Blender, with or without the add-on. Atlas tasks
themselves always run through the `worldlabs` CLI below, or through the add-on.

With only connected World Labs tools and no shell, the task tools take the same requests. The
depth files usually cannot be read there, so cameras are placed without measuring: stay near
space the image clearly shows as open, generate a few views at a time, and look at each result.

## 1. Pose the images

Upload each image, estimate its camera and depth, and save the result:

```sh
worldlabs assets upload room.jpg --json                    # note the "id"
echo '{"frames":[{"imageAsset":{"assetId":"<id>"}}],"targetResolution":[1280,720]}' > pose.json
worldlabs tasks run images2PosedRGBD --request pose.json --wait --json > pose_op.json
worldlabs operations download <pose-operation-id> --out scene
```

- `targetResolution` sets the grid every later step uses. Choose the size closest to the image's
  shape: `[1280, 720]`, `[960, 720]`, `[528, 704]` or `[720, 1280]`.
- Photos of one real place go in one request, so their cameras share a world.
- Posing puts the scene in a level, Y-up world. Pose an image from `atlasTextToImage` as well: the
  depth that task can return is not levelled.
- `scene/operation.json` holds each frame's camera, and for its image, depth and confidence the
  local `path` and the `assetId`. Later requests name frames by those asset IDs; nothing is
  uploaded again.

## 2. See the scene

Look at the scene before placing anything, and look at it as a picture, not only as numbers. In
Blender the posed frames are cameras with point clouds. In a shell, draw the depth points from
above with the camera on them; walls, furniture and open floor show at a glance.

Find how far away things are, where the floor is, and where there is room to stand. Distances
are in the depth's units, which is what tells you how big a move is. Settle with the person what
the main part of the scene is.

## 3. Build the scene out

One image is a single view of a place. This step decides what the rest of the place is: the far
side of the table, the wall behind the camera, what is round the corner. The model invents
whatever a camera sees that no frame has shown, and here that is the point. A round takes under
a minute, and you and the person see the result before anything is built on it.

Explore the way a person would walk into a room they had only seen in a photo: go in, cross to
the other side, turn round and look back. At this stage the question is what is in this place,
not where a camera path or a viewer will go. That comes after, and it will be better for having
a real scene to choose from.

Work in rounds:

1. **Place a few cameras** that stand somewhere no frame has stood and look at something no
   frame has shown: from one side of the main subject across to the other, from the far end
   back toward where the first camera stood, into a corner, through an opening.
2. **Generate them** as one `atlasGenerate` request, with the frames so far as `contextFrames`
   and `"returnDepth": true`, so each new view joins the scene with its own depth.
3. **Look at what came back.** Each view shows new surfaces and new open space. Drop a view that
   disagrees with the others.
4. **Place the next few** from what the new views revealed: floor that turned out to be open, a

later rounds pass the frames nearest the new cameras as context, not every frame. The

quick.

content.content:
# Billing

Understand credits, projects, spend limits, and payments.

Atlas Developer API usage is billed to the account that owns the API key's
project. Balances, top-ups, and monthly spend limits are under
[Settings → Developer Platform](https://atlas.worldlabs.ai/settings/credits/developer). Payment methods and
invoices are under [Settings → Billing](https://atlas.worldlabs.ai/settings/billing). Account usage is on the
[Settings → Usage](https://atlas.worldlabs.ai/settings/usage/developer) page.

## Credits and top-ups

Developer API tasks draw credits from the account balance. The current
conversion is 1,000 credits per US dollar. Credits purchased for the account
do not expire.

Account owners and billing owners can add credits manually or enable automatic
recharge. Auto-recharge charges the account's default payment method when the
balance falls below a configured threshold and restores it to the chosen
balance.

The task rate card can change. Use the current rate card shown in
the platform when estimating task costs rather than embedding model prices in
client code.

## Frameboy sessions

A Frameboy session in Atlas Studio runs for up to a minute and costs 500
credits ($0.50), charged once, after it ends. It draws on the same credits as
other Studio work. A session is free if it plays for less than 5 seconds, or if
it ends because its server stopped responding.

An account without enough credits cannot start a session: the request returns
`402 Payment Required` with `code` set to `CREDITS_UNAVAILABLE`, and no session
is started or queued. A charge can take a few minutes to appear on the Usage
page.

## Studio tools

Prompt enhancement costs 20 credits ($0.02) a request. An image edit costs 125
credits ($0.125) a request. An image upscale costs 10 credits ($0.01) an image.
A Chisel caption costs 20 credits ($0.02) a request. A Relight image edit costs
what the model provider charged for it, converted to credits.

## Projects and attribution

Create projects to separate credentials, assets, operations, and usage for
different environments or products. Every API key is bound to one project, so
usage is attributed without sending a project ID in each Developer API route.

Project isolation is useful even when one account funds all work:

- production and development can use different keys;
- teams can inspect their own usage;
- experiments can receive a tighter budget;
- a compromised key cannot access another project's resources.

## Usage

The Usage page shows the credits the account spent over a date range, per day
and grouped by task or project. Developer API usage can also be grouped by API
key. Studio and Developer usage are shown separately. Select a day to see its
breakdown. Usage reflects billed charges; a finished task can take a few
minutes to appear.

## Set monthly spend limits

Account owners and billing owners can create a monthly USD spend limit for the
entire account or for one project. Limits reset each calendar month.

When an enabled applicable limit reaches 100%, new Developer API tasks pause.
Tasks already running are allowed to finish. Raising, disabling, or deleting
the limit allows new tasks once the account also has sufficient credits.

Use an account-wide limit for the total safety ceiling, then add project limits
for workloads that need independent guardrails. A project task must satisfy
both limits when both apply.

> Spend limits are guardrails, not exact real-time accounting boundaries.
> In-flight work and delayed usage observations can produce some variance.

## Payment methods and invoices

The account uses one shared Stripe payment profile for API credit purchases,
automatic recharge, and Atlas Studio subscriptions. Account owners and
billing owners can add a payment method, choose the default, open the Stripe
customer portal, and review invoices from the billing page.

Do not put payment operations in an API integration. Billing administration
uses the authenticated platform session and account permissions, not a World
Labs API key.

## When work is paused

If a task is rejected because the account is out of credits or a spend limit is
reached, the response is `402 Payment Required` with `code` set to
`CREDITS_UNAVAILABLE` or `SPEND_LIMIT_EXCEEDED`:

1. Do not retry in a tight loop.
2. Check the API key's project limit and the account-wide limit.
3. Add credits or adjust the appropriate limit.
4. Retry the same logical submission with its original idempotency key.

method.description:
Action to specify what pull request data needs to be retrieved from GitHub. 
Possible options: 
 1. get - Get details of a specific pull request.
 2. get_diff - Get the diff of a pull request.
 3. get_status - Get combined commit status of a head commit in a pull request.
 4. get_files - Get the list of files changed in a pull request. Use with pagination parameters to control the number of results returned.
 5. get_commits - Get the list of commits on a pull request. Use with pagination parameters to control the number of results returned.
 6. get_review_comments - Get review threads on a pull request. Each thread contains logically grouped review comments made on the same code location during pull request reviews. Returns thread metadata and comments with nullable current and original line-range coordinates (line, start_line, original_line, original_start_line). Current coordinates are omitted when unavailable, such as for outdated comments. Use cursor-based pagination (perPage, after) to control results.
 7. get_reviews - Get the reviews on a pull request. When asked for review comments, use get_review_comments method. Use with pagination parameters to control the number of results returned.
 8. get_comments - Get comments on a pull request. Use this if user doesn't specifically want review comments. Use with pagination parameters to control the number of results returned.
 9. get_check_runs - Get check runs for the head commit of a pull request. Check runs are the individual CI/CD jobs and checks that run on the PR.

perPage.description: Results per page for pagination (min 1, max 100)
